warmup.q: In the report service, one thread only ever writes stats.parsed (documents parsed), and another only ever writes stats.written (reports written). Both fields are volatile long in the same small object. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: they never touch the same field, so there's no contention
Lost updates, because ++ on a volatile isn't atomic
Both threads can slow down, because the two fields share a cache line that the cores keep taking from each other
A deadlock between the two threads
warmup.why: Caches move memory in 64-byte lines, and a core that writes a line needs the only copy. Two fields 8 bytes apart sit on one line, so every write by one thread invalidates the other core's copy, and the other way round. Nothing is lost: each field has a single writer, so ++ on it is safe. How much time it costs depends on the machine, as the section on false sharing shows.

opening:
Picture two cooks at one counter, sharing a single cutting board. One chops onions, the other chops peppers. They never touch each other's vegetables, so there's nothing to argue about. But only one knife fits on the board at a time, so each cook keeps stepping back to wait for the other.

Your processor has the same problem in miniature. Two threads, two lines of work running at the same time, can slow each other down even when each writes only its own field. The two fields share one small block of memory, and the hardware moves that block around as a unit.

It's an easy trap, because the code looks perfect: no shared data, no locks, no race. And this time the JIT isn't involved at all; the cost lives in the hardware. Lesson 3 gave us honest benchmarks on one thread; now a second thread joins. In this lesson, we'll see how caches move memory, read real field offsets, set two counters fighting over one line, pad them apart, and meet the JDK's own answer, LongAdder. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two cooks who never touch each other's vegetables and still keep waiting, because they share one cutting board. Two threads that write two fields on one cache line do the same, and padding, a chain of classes or LongAdder's padded cells give each its own board. How much it costs depends on the machine, so measure where you run.

Now look in your code for an array or object where each thread writes its own slot or field in a busy loop. Slots 8 bytes apart share a line.

Next, we'll stop guessing where a running program spends its time: how can the JDK Flight Recorder log what the JVM was doing, on one clock, cheaply enough to leave on?

sections.html:
A processor never reads a single long from memory on its own. Main memory is far away, as distances inside a computer go. So each core, one of the processor's units that runs a thread, keeps small, fast memories close by: its caches (called L1 and L2). They don't hold single variables. They hold cache lines, blocks of 64 bytes on x86 processors. The course machine says so directly: the file /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/coherency_line_size contains 64.

A cache line is the cutting board: a fixed-size surface where the work happens. The hardware moves the whole board, never a single onion.

Each core keeps its own copy of any line it uses, and the hardware keeps the copies in step. That's cache coherence, which the memory model track met as the reason caches don't serve stale values. Coherence has a price, though. A core that wants to write a line needs the only valid copy of it. Every other core's copy is marked invalid, and the next time one of those cores touches the line, it has to fetch it again.

Now look at an ordinary object in memory. The report service works in two stages: a parser reads each document, and a writer produces its report. It counts what each stage has done. JOL (Java Object Layout), a small OpenJDK library, reads the real field offsets from the running JVM. An offset is a field's distance in bytes from the start of the object:

Java
static final class Adjacent {
    volatile long parsed;     // written only by the parsing thread
    volatile long written;    // written only by the writing thread
}
// JOL on JDK 21 and JDK 25: 32 bytes; parsed at offset 16, written at offset 24
Kotlin
class KAdjacent {
    @Volatile var parsed = 0L     // written only by the parsing thread
    @Volatile var written = 0L    // written only by the writing thread
}
// JOL on JDK 21 and JDK 25: 32 bytes; parsed at offset 16, written at offset 24

(volatile makes each write visible to other threads at once, as the memory model track showed.) The first 12 bytes are the object header: 8 bytes of bookkeeping and a 4-byte pointer to the object's class. Then come 4 bytes of gap, so the longs start on an 8-byte boundary, and then the two fields, 8 bytes apart. The whole object is 32 bytes. Unless it happens to straddle the edge of a line, both counters sit on the same 64-byte line: the same board.

For code that reads, that's good news. Reading parsed brings written along for free, and arrays of numbers are fast to scan for the same reason. For two threads that each write their own field, it's bad news, as the next section shows.

Offsets depend on the JVM and its flags. On JDK 25 with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders (JEP 519), the header shrinks to 8 bytes, and LayoutDemo then shows parsed at 8 and written at 16 in a 24-byte object. JDK 27 turns compact headers on by default (JEP 534). So when you check a layout in a test, check the distance between fields, never their absolute offsets.

Memory moves in 64-byte lines, not in fields. Fields 8 bytes apart travel together.

Two counters on one line cost nothing while one thread reads them. Let's give each of them a writer of its own.

try.title: Read real layouts with JOL
steps: Before you run anything, predict the offset of written in each of the three classes in LayoutDemo.
Run LayoutDemo. Ignore JOL's two # WARNING lines about attaching to the JVM.
Look at the last entry: Striped64$Cell, the class LongAdder uses inside. Where is its only field?
Run the Kotlin twin and compare.

code.title: LayoutDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l04; import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout; /** Prints the real field layout of four classes with JOL: where each field sits, in bytes. */ public class LayoutDemo { static final class Adjacent { volatile long parsed; volatile long written; } static final class PaddedInOneClass { // padding fields between the counters volatile long parsed; long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8, p9, p10, p11, p12, p13, p14, p15, p16; volatile long written; } static class ParsedField { volatile long parsed; } // superclass fields are laid out first static class Pad1 extends ParsedField { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } static class WrittenField extends Pad1 { volatile long written; } static final class Padded extends WrittenField { long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7, q8; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { print(Adjacent.class); print(PaddedInOneClass.class); print(Padded.class); // the cell behind LongAdder: the JDK pads it with @Contended print(Class.forName("java.util.concurrent.atomic.Striped64$Cell")); } static void print(Class<?> type) { ClassLayout layout = ClassLayout.parseClass(type); System.out.println(type.getSimpleName() + ": " + layout.instanceSize() + " bytes"); layout.fields().stream() .filter(f -> f.name().equals("parsed") || f.name().equals("written") || f.name().equals("value")) .forEach(f -> System.out.printf(" %-7s at offset %3d%n", f.name(), f.offset())); } }

alt.title: LayoutDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l04 import org.openjdk.jol.info.ClassLayout // Kotlin twin of LayoutDemo.java: the same layouts, declared in Kotlin. // @Volatile var compiles to a volatile field, so JOL sees the same thing as in Java. class KAdjacent { @Volatile var parsed = 0L @Volatile var written = 0L } open class KParsedField { @Volatile var parsed = 0L } // superclass fields are laid out first open class KPad1 : KParsedField() { var p1 = 0L; var p2 = 0L; var p3 = 0L; var p4 = 0L; var p5 = 0L; var p6 = 0L; var p7 = 0L; var p8 = 0L } open class KWrittenField : KPad1() { @Volatile var written = 0L } class KPadded : KWrittenField() { var q1 = 0L; var q2 = 0L; var q3 = 0L; var q4 = 0L; var q5 = 0L; var q6 = 0L; var q7 = 0L; var q8 = 0L } fun main() { printLayout(KAdjacent::class.java) printLayout(KPadded::class.java) // the cell behind LongAdder: the JDK pads it with @Contended printLayout(Class.forName("java.util.concurrent.atomic.Striped64\$Cell")) } fun printLayout(type: Class<*>) { val layout = ClassLayout.parseClass(type) println("${type.simpleName}: ${layout.instanceSize()} bytes") layout.fields() .filter { it.name() in setOf("parsed", "written", "value") } .forEach { println(" %-7s at offset %3d".format(it.name(), it.offset())) } }

try.expect: On JDK 21 and JDK 25: Adjacent is 32 bytes with parsed at 16 and written at 24. PaddedInOneClass is 160 bytes with written at 152. Padded, built from a chain of classes, is 160 bytes with written at 88, 72 bytes after parsed. Cell is 152 bytes, and its value field sits at offset 144: the JDK pads it on purpose. Kotlin's @Volatile var fields get exactly the same layout. With -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders on JDK 25, every offset moves down by 8 and every distance stays the same. On JDK 25, JOL also prints warnings about sun.misc.Unsafe, which it uses internally.

sections.h: False sharing: two threads, two fields, one line
sections.html:
The parsing thread now writes only parsed, and the writing thread writes only written. They share no data, so there's nothing to lock and no race, no two threads writing the same variable. But they share a line, and the line can live in only one core's cache for writing at a time.

Trace two writes. Core 1 holds the line and adds 1 to parsed. Core 2 wants to add 1 to written, finds its copy invalid, and waits while the line travels over. Now core 1's copy is invalid, so its next parsed++ waits for the line to travel back. Each ++ is a few nanoseconds of work wrapped in a wait. When both threads run at the same moment, the line bounces between the cores on almost every write. This is false sharing: the program shares nothing, and the hardware shares a lot. The figure shows the bounce.

FalseSharingDemo runs exactly that, 25 million increments per thread: first with the adjacent fields, then with the fields padded apart. Before you read on, decide what you expect. Here is one run on the busy course machine:

round 1: adjacent   994 ms   padded   785 ms
round 2: adjacent   977 ms   padded   784 ms
round 3: adjacent 1,124 ms   padded   806 ms

That's a gap, but a small one, and it wasn't even steady. Across nine runs here, in Java and Kotlin, the padded version lost one round in three. Was the mechanism wrong? No. More than 20 other busy programs were sharing the machine's four cores, so our two threads were rarely running at the same moment. A line can only bounce between two cores that both want it right now. When this lesson was first written, on a quieter day, the same demo on the same machine told the textbook story: adjacent took 957 to 1,387 ms and padded 206 to 247 ms, about five times faster.

Where the threads run matters too. Two hyperthreads, two hardware threads that share one physical core, also share that core's L1 and L2 caches. Put the two writers there, and there's no line to bounce at all.

So don't promise anyone a speed-up from padding. The mechanism is certain, and the size of the effect isn't. The only way to know is to measure on the hardware you run on, under the load you run with. When it does hit, it hits code that looks perfectly innocent: a stats object with one counter per worker thread, or an array of per-thread totals whose slots sit 8 bytes apart.

Separate fields aren't separate memory. Fields that different threads write in a hot loop need lines of their own.

The cure, when you need it, is space between the fields. Java makes that a little harder than it sounds.

try.title: Race two counters on one line
steps: Read FalseSharingDemo. Predict: will the adjacent run be slower, the same, or faster than the padded one on your machine?
Close other busy programs if you can. Run it, then run it again. Then run the Kotlin twin.
If you see a big gap, check how many physical cores your machine has (lscpu on Linux, sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu on macOS). If you see none, check how busy the machine is (uptime shows the load).

code.title: FalseSharingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l04; /** * Two threads, each incrementing its OWN volatile counter 25 million times: one counts the * documents the report service has parsed, the other the reports it has written. * Run 1: the two counters sit next to each other. Run 2: they are padded apart. * Whether you see a difference depends on your CPU and where the OS puts the threads. */ public class FalseSharingDemo { // the two counters in one 32-byte object: almost certainly on the same 64-byte cache line static final class Adjacent { volatile long parsed; volatile long written; } // superclass fields come first, so the padding class sits between parsed and written static class ParsedField { volatile long parsed; } static class Pad1 extends ParsedField { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } static class WrittenField extends Pad1 { volatile long written; } static final class Padded extends WrittenField { long q1, q2, q3, q4, q5, q6, q7, q8; } static final int N = 25_000_000; static long run(Runnable a, Runnable b) throws InterruptedException { Thread t1 = new Thread(a), t2 = new Thread(b); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { Adjacent adj = new Adjacent(); long msAdjacent = run(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) adj.parsed++; }, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) adj.written++; }); Padded pad = new Padded(); long msPadded = run(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pad.parsed++; }, () -> { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pad.written++; }); System.out.printf("round %d: adjacent %,5d ms padded %,5d ms (counts %d/%d, %d/%d)%n", round, msAdjacent, msPadded, adj.parsed, adj.written, pad.parsed, pad.written); } } }

alt.title: FalseSharingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of FalseSharingDemo.java: two threads, each incrementing its OWN volatile counter // (documents parsed, reports written). // Run 1: the counters sit next to each other. Run 2: they are padded apart (KPadded from LayoutDemo.kt). // Whether you see a difference depends on your CPU and where the OS puts the threads. private const val N = 25_000_000 private fun timeTwo(a: () -> Unit, b: () -> Unit): Long { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val t1 = thread { a() } val t2 = thread { b() } t1.join(); t2.join() return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val adj = KAdjacent() val msAdjacent = timeTwo({ repeat(N) { adj.parsed++ } }, { repeat(N) { adj.written++ } }) val pad = KPadded() val msPadded = timeTwo({ repeat(N) { pad.parsed++ } }, { repeat(N) { pad.written++ } }) println("round %d: adjacent %,5d ms padded %,5d ms (counts %d/%d, %d/%d)" .format(round, msAdjacent, msPadded, adj.parsed, adj.written, pad.parsed, pad.written)) } }

try.expect: On a laptop with several physical cores and little else running, the adjacent run is often several times slower than the padded one. On a busy machine you may see a small gap, none, or the reverse, as the course machine did (about 1,000 ms against 800 ms, with some rounds reversed). All four counts always end at exactly 25,000,000: false sharing costs time, never correctness.

sections.h: Padding pushes hot fields onto separate lines
sections.html:
The fix is to keep at least 64 bytes between fields that different threads write: give each cook a board of their own. Padding means unused bytes placed between fields for exactly that reason. There are three ways to add it.

The first is padding fields inside one class: 8 or more unused longs between parsed and written. On today's HotSpot it works (written moved to offset 152), but JMH's false-sharing sample warns that this is "not versatile because JVMs can freely rearrange the field order, even of the same type".

The second is a chain of classes. The same sample notes that "superclass fields are usually laid out first". So put each hot field and each block of padding in a class of its own, and chain them, each class extending the one before:

Java
abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; }
abstract class PadAfterParsed extends ParsedCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; }
abstract class WrittenCounter extends PadAfterParsed { volatile long written; }

public final class StageCounters extends WrittenCounter {
    public void addParsed() { parsed++; }      // only the parsing thread calls this
    public void addWritten() { written++; }    // only the writing thread calls this
}
Kotlin
abstract class ParsedCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var parsed = 0L }
abstract class PadAfterParsed : ParsedCounter() {
    @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L
    @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L
}
abstract class WrittenCounter : PadAfterParsed() { @Volatile @JvmField var written = 0L }

class StageCounters : WrittenCounter() {
    fun addParsed() { parsed++ }               // only the parsing thread calls this
    fun addWritten() { written++ }             // only the writing thread calls this
}

This is the shape the lab asks for. @JvmField in the Kotlin version makes each property a plain public field, which keeps the layout easy to read.

The third is @Contended, the JDK's own annotation, jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended, available since JDK 8. The JVM adds ContendedPaddingWidth bytes of padding, 128 by default, around each annotated field. On JDK 25, JOL on a class with both counters annotated showed parsed at offset 144, written at 280, and a 288-byte object. Its Javadoc warns that it "will nearly always add significant space overhead to objects".

There are two catches for your own classes. First, the JVM ignores the annotation outside the JDK unless you run with -XX:-RestrictContended. Without that flag, JOL showed the same 16 and 24 as no annotation at all, and the JVM printed no warning. It simply ignores you, politely. Second, the annotation lives in an internal package, so compiling needs --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED. javac refuses that together with --release: "exporting a package from system module java.base is not allowed with --release". This course's labs compile with --release 21, so they can't use it.

Every kind of padding costs memory: 160 bytes instead of 32 here, and 288 with @Contended. That's nothing for one counter object and a lot for a million of them.

Padding costs memory on every object. Pad the few that several threads write in a hot loop, and check their offsets.

Check yourself: a class declares volatile long a;, then seven padding longs, then volatile long b;. JOL shows a at 16 and b at 80. Can they share a line? (No: they're 64 bytes apart. But another JVM may order the fields differently, which is why the lab's test reads the real offsets instead of trusting the source.)

Hand padding is fiddly, costs memory and leans on JVM habits. For the most common case, a counter that many threads bump, the JDK has already done all of it.

sections.h: LongAdder: the padding the JDK already did for you
sections.html:
Hand padding is for library authors. For a counter in your own code, use LongAdder. LongAdder (and its sibling LongAccumulator) extends Striped64, whose source explains the design. Its table entries are a "variant of AtomicLong padded (via @Contended) to reduce cache contention", because "Atomic objects residing in arrays will tend to be placed adjacent to each other, and so will most often share cache lines (with a huge negative performance impact) without this precaution". That's the value at offset 144 you saw in LayoutDemo.

In the kitchen, it's each cook keeping a tally of dishes on a slip by their own board, and the manager adding the slips up at closing time.

The slips are only handed out when needed. The source says: "When there is no contention, all updates are made to the base field." Contention means threads getting in each other's way. Here it's a failed compare-and-set. Compare-and-set is the "update it only if nobody beat me to it" instruction behind AtomicLong, the JDK's thread-safe counter, and it fails when another thread changed the value first. On the first failed compare-and-set, LongAdder creates a table of 2 cells, and it doubles the table under more contention. Each thread then mostly updates its own cell, on its own line. sum() adds up the base and the cells. As "Atomics and compare-and-set" said, sum() is not an atomic snapshot. So use LongAdder for counters you read now and then, such as metrics, and AtomicLong when the value drives a decision.

Here's the report service's request counter, the one the lab fixes. Every request thread calls record once per report, and a monitoring program reads the totals every few seconds:

Java
public final class RequestMetrics {
    private final LongAdder count = new LongAdder();
    private final LongAdder totalWords = new LongAdder();

    public void record(long words) {          // called by every request thread
        count.increment();
        totalWords.add(words);
    }

    public long count() { return count.sum(); }   // read by the monitoring program
}
Kotlin
class RequestMetrics {
    private val count = LongAdder()
    private val totalWords = LongAdder()

    fun record(words: Long) {                  // called by every request thread
        count.increment()
        totalWords.add(words)
    }

    fun count(): Long = count.sum()            // read by the monitoring program
}

AdderDemo races the two kinds of counter: four threads count 10 million requests each, first into one AtomicLong, then into one LongAdder. On the busy course machine, the race came out backwards:

round 1: AtomicLong   705 ms (40,000,000)   LongAdder 1,320 ms (40,000,000)
round 2: AtomicLong   693 ms (40,000,000)   LongAdder 1,144 ms (40,000,000)
round 3: AtomicLong   680 ms (40,000,000)   LongAdder 1,156 ms (40,000,000)

Both counts are exact, as they always are. The speed tells the false-sharing story again. With 20 other programs competing for four cores, our four threads mostly took turns, so their compare-and-sets rarely failed, and LongAdder paid for bookkeeping it didn't need. On the quieter day when this lesson was first written, the same demo gave AtomicLong 640 to 760 ms per round and LongAdder about 200 ms. With four threads really running at once, all four cores fought over the AtomicLong's single line, and LongAdder let each of them work on its own padded cell.

This is also where the cutting-board picture breaks. A cook who waits for the board notices, and it costs seconds. A core waits nanoseconds for a line, and nobody notices until it happens a few hundred million times. That's why you measure instead of guessing.

Many writers and rare readers: count with LongAdder. When the value drives a decision, use AtomicLong.

We can now measure a piece of code carefully, but only a piece we already suspect. A real program has thousands of methods, so the next question is how to catch a running JVM in the act.

try.title: AtomicLong against LongAdder
steps: Predict which one finishes first with four threads, and by how much.
Change THREADS to 1 and run again. Does LongAdder still win?

code.title: AdderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Four threads count 10 million report requests each, into one AtomicLong and then into one LongAdder. */ public class AdderDemo { static final int THREADS = 4, PER_THREAD = 10_000_000; static long time(Runnable perThread) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int i = 0; i < THREADS; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } perThread.run(); }); ts[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); long msAtomic = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long msAdder = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)%n", round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum()); } } }

alt.title: AdderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l04 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of AdderDemo.java: four threads count 10 million report requests each, // into one AtomicLong and then into one LongAdder. private const val THREADS = 4 private const val PER_THREAD = 10_000_000 private fun timeAll(perThread: () -> Unit): Long { val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(THREADS) { thread { go.await(); perThread() } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val atomic = AtomicLong() val msAtomic = timeAll { repeat(PER_THREAD) { atomic.incrementAndGet() } } val adder = LongAdder() val msAdder = timeAll { repeat(PER_THREAD) { adder.increment() } } println("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)" .format(round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum())) } }

try.expect: Both always count exactly 40,000,000. With four threads on a machine with free cores, LongAdder usually finishes well ahead. On a busy machine it can lose, as it did on the course machine (about 690 ms against 1,150 ms). With one thread, the counts are 10,000,000 and AtomicLong wins: 103 ms against 181 ms in the last round on the course machine. With no contention, LongAdder only touches its base field, its cells never exist, and its extra checks are pure cost.

compare.title: A padded counter in Java and Kotlin

java.title: StageCounters.java
java.html: abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; } abstract class PadAfterParsed extends ParsedCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } abstract class WrittenCounter extends PadAfterParsed { volatile long written; } public final class StageCounters extends WrittenCounter { public void addParsed() { parsed++; } // only the parsing thread calls this public void addWritten() { written++; } // only the writing thread calls this }

kotlin.title: StageCounters.kt
kotlin.html: abstract class ParsedCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var parsed = 0L } abstract class PadAfterParsed : ParsedCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class WrittenCounter : PadAfterParsed() { @Volatile @JvmField var written = 0L } class StageCounters : WrittenCounter() { fun addParsed() { parsed++ } // only the parsing thread calls this fun addWritten() { written++ } // only the writing thread calls this }

compare.note: Both compile to the same JVM classes with the same field layout, because the JVM decides the layout, not the language. The differences are in what you write. Kotlin classes are final by default, so the padding classes need abstract or open. A Kotlin var property is a private field plus a getter and a setter; @JvmField exposes the field directly, and @Volatile makes it volatile. In both languages the padding fields are never read, and nothing in either language promises the order of fields within one class, which is why the chain of classes is the safer trick.

worked.title: Find false sharing in a stats object and fix it

steps.say: The report service has two worker threads, and each updates its own counter in one shared stats object. A profile shows both threads spending time in record, which does almost nothing. Start by printing the layout.
steps.code: System.out.println(ClassLayout.parseClass(WorkerStats.class).toPrintable());

alt.html: println(ClassLayout.parseClass(WorkerStats::class.java).toPrintable())

steps.say: The two hot fields are 8 bytes apart. Worker 0 writes done0, worker 1 writes done1, and both sit on one line. This is JOL's real output on JDK 25.
steps.code:
OFF  SZ   TYPE DESCRIPTION               VALUE
  0   8        (object header: mark)     N/A
  8   4        (object header: class)    N/A
 12   4        (alignment/padding gap)   
 16   8   long WorkerStats.done0         N/A
 24   8   long WorkerStats.done1         N/A
Instance size: 32 bytes

steps.say: Give each worker its own object instead of padding one. Two WorkerCounter objects created one after the other can still end up next to each other in memory, so if the profile still shows the problem, pad the counter class or use a LongAdder. Self-check: why don't separate objects guarantee separate lines? (Answer: each thread gets new objects from its own stretch of the heap, one after another, so two small objects created together are often only a few bytes apart.)
steps.code: final class WorkerCounter { volatile long done; // one writer: the worker's own thread } WorkerCounter[] counters = { new WorkerCounter(), new WorkerCounter() };

alt.html: class WorkerCounter { @Volatile var done = 0L // one writer: the worker's own thread } val counters = arrayOf(WorkerCounter(), WorkerCounter())

steps.say: Verify with a forked JMH benchmark that runs two threads, on the hardware and under the load you deploy to, not on your laptop alone. Keep the version that measures faster there. If neither is clearly faster, keep the simpler code.

lab.title: Pad two counters and fix a metrics counter
steps: Open StageCounters, the report service's two counters: parsed, written only by the parsing thread, and written, written only by the writing thread. Then open RequestMetrics, which every request thread calls once per report. Run the tests. Three of four fail: parsed and written are 8 bytes apart (at 16 and 24), and RequestMetrics loses updates when 8 threads record at once.
Lay out StageCounters so parsed and written are at least 64 bytes apart. Keep both fields volatile long with those exact names, and keep the public methods. A chain of classes is the reliable way.
Fix RequestMetrics so count() and totalWords() are exact under contention. Writes happen on every request and reads every few seconds, so pick the tool built for that.
Run the tests until all four pass. Run them twice: the metrics tests are race tests.
Optional: print ClassLayout.parseClass(StageCounters.class).toPrintable() in a scratch test and look at your layout.
hints: HotSpot lays out superclass fields before subclass fields. abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; }, then a class with eight long padding fields extending it, then a class with written extending that, and StageCounters at the end of the chain.
The fields in the superclasses can't be private if StageCounters needs to read them. Package-private works, and JOL finds fields in superclasses too.

count++ on a volatile is a read and a write, so two threads can both read 41 and both write 42. With many writers, LongAdder.increment() and add(words) are exact and spread the writes over padded cells.
The reference solution puts written 72 bytes after parsed and passes on JDK 21 and JDK 25.
lab.done: All four tests in CacheLineTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Explain a layout and write the fix from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. JOL prints parsed at offset 16 and written at offset 24 for a class that two threads write. Write two sentences on what goes wrong and why, then write a padded version using a chain of classes. Then write the one-line answer you'd give for a request counter written by 200 threads.

answer.html: // parsed and written are 8 bytes apart, so they share one 64-byte cache line. Each write by one // core invalidates the other core's copy, so the line bounces between them (false sharing). abstract class ParsedCounter { volatile long parsed; } abstract class PadAfterParsed extends ParsedCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } abstract class WrittenCounter extends PadAfterParsed { volatile long written; } public final class StageCounters extends WrittenCounter { } // 200 writers, occasional reads: use a LongAdder private final LongAdder requests = new LongAdder();

alt.html: // parsed and written are 8 bytes apart, so they share one 64-byte cache line. Each write by one // core invalidates the other core's copy, so the line bounces between them (false sharing). abstract class ParsedCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var parsed = 0L } abstract class PadAfterParsed : ParsedCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class WrittenCounter : PadAfterParsed() { @Volatile @JvmField var written = 0L } class StageCounters : WrittenCounter() // 200 writers, occasional reads: use a LongAdder private val requests = LongAdder()

recap: Caches move memory in 64-byte lines, and a core that writes a line invalidates every other core's copy.

False sharing: two threads writing different fields on the same line make it bounce between cores. It costs time, never correctness, and how much depends on the hardware and on whether the threads really run at once.

Pad hot fields at least 64 bytes apart. A chain of classes is reliable; padding fields in one class may be reordered; @Contended needs -XX:-RestrictContended and an internal export for your own classes.
Check layouts with JOL and assert distances, not offsets: headers differ between JDKs and flags (compact object headers are the default in JDK 27).
For counters in your own code, use LongAdder: its cells are padded with @Contended and only created under contention. Without contention, AtomicLong is a little faster.
The limit: everything here makes one known hot spot cheaper. None of it tells you where a running program actually spends its time; that's what the profilers in the next lessons are for.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why giving each worker thread its own field in a shared stats object didn't make the counters fast, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: The fields are separate, so there's no race, but they sit 8 bytes apart, which puts them on the same 64-byte cache line. A core can only write a line it holds alone, so each write by one thread invalidates the other core's copy, and the line moves back and forth on almost every update. That's false sharing. One fix is to pad the fields at least 64 bytes apart, ideally with a chain of classes because the JVM may reorder fields within one class, and to check the offsets with JOL. For ordinary counters I'd use a LongAdder per counter instead: it creates padded cells only when threads contend and adds them up when we read. And I'd only believe a speed-up after measuring it on our real hardware under real load, because how much false sharing costs depends on the CPU and on whether the threads truly run at the same time.

deeper.html:
JMH protects you from one source of false sharing automatically. Its false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your @State object can still share a line, which is exactly what that sample demonstrates, with several fixes side by side. To measure it on your own hardware, run that sample with several forks on a machine with real cores and little else running.

Why does the JDK pad with 128 bytes when lines are 64? The flag ContendedPaddingWidth only says how many bytes to pad. A common explanation is that some processors also fetch the neighbouring line, so a 64-byte gap can still let two hot fields interfere. This course couldn't check that against a primary source, so treat 128 as "the JDK's safe default" rather than a rule.

Two other tools look at the same problem from the hardware side. perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines that bounce between cores (JMH wraps it as -prof perfc2c). And a CPU profiler such as async-profiler, in lesson 6, shows the symptom: lots of samples on a trivial line such as count++.

There's also true sharing, which padding can't fix: many threads writing the same field, like an AtomicLong hit by every request. The only fixes there are to write less often or to split the value, which is what LongAdder does.
